extracted.intended_audience: state regulators, power plant operators, industry stakeholders, environmental lawyers, and public commenters on EPA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and methodological guidance used by EPA to set achievable performance standards (BSER), calculate emissions rates, and estimate costs for electric generating units (EGUs) under CAA section 111, including CCS applicability, turbine-class benchmarks, cost/economic assumptions, and CO2 transport/storage reporting expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER defined as CCS with 90 percent capture
rubrics_metrics.description: “The EPA uses the two phrases (i) BSER is CCS with 90 percent capture and (ii) CCS with 90 percent capture is achievable, or similar phrases, interchangeably.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA treats CCS with ~90% capture as the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for applicable subcategory(ies); the phraseology may be used interchangeably in the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER applicability for non-base load combustion turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: “The EPA proposed that because the BSER for non-base load combustion turbines was simple cycle technology, CCS was not applicable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether CCS is considered applicable depends on the EGU subcategory (e.g., non-base load simple-cycle combustion turbines may be excluded from CCS-based BSER).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for CCS auxiliary load when reporting net output and percent reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements showing CCS reduces net output (e.g., NETL F-class combined cycle EGU without CCS is 726 MW; auxiliary load with CCS reduces net output to 645 MW; H-class without CCS is 992 MW; with CCS to 883 MW).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emissions reductions from CCS must account for increased auxiliary parasitic loads that reduce net electrical output; numeric percent reductions (e.g., 89%) reflect this reduced net output and rounding may cause slight numeric mismatches when applying percent reductions to phase-1 standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost estimation economic assumptions and treatment of CCS costs
rubrics_metrics.description: “These calculations use a service life of 30 years, an interest rate of 7.0 percent, a natural gas price of $3.61/MMBtu, and a capacity factor of 65 percent. These costs do not include CO2 transport, storage, or monitoring costs.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA (in the referenced calculations) specifies explicit economic assumptions (service life, discount rate, fuel price, capacity factor) and excludes CO2 transport/storage/monitoring from those cost figures unless otherwise noted. Use of these parameters (or stated alternatives) should be documented when performing or evaluating cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different amortization periods for CCS equipment depending on tax-credit window
rubrics_metrics.description: “The CCS and CO2 TS&M costs are amortized over the period the equipment is operated—30 years or 12 years.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For coal-fired existing units EPA used a 12-year amortization for CCS equipment to reflect operation during the 45Q tax-credit availability; new-build assumptions may use 30-year amortization. Amortization choice materially affects levelized compliance costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of higher initial capacity factor for first 12 years to reflect 45Q effects
rubrics_metrics.description: “For this final rule, the EPA considers the approach of using a higher capacity factor for the first 12 years and a lower one for the last 18 years to reflect more accurately actual operating conditions, and therefore to be a more realistic basis for calculating CCS costs.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost and compliance calculations can use a time-varying capacity factor (higher during the tax-credit window, lower afterward) rather than a constant value to better reflect economics under 45Q; this reduces apparent compliance costs relative to a constant-capacity-factor approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative turbine-class selection and normalization approach
rubrics_metrics.description: “the 6,100 MMBtu/h H-Class combustion turbine is the median size of recently constructed combined cycle facilities and the 4,600 MMBtu/h F-Class combustion turbine approximates the size of a number of recently constructed combined cycle facilities as well.... As noted in RTC section 3.1, we expect costs to decrease due to learning by doing and technological development. ... larger more efficient combined cycle turbine will operate as base load combustion turbines.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA benchmarks achievable performance using representative NETL H-class and F-class turbine models (median/typical sizes) and applies normalization assumptions (including a linear relationship for turbines <2,000 MMBtu/h) when estimating achievable emissions and costs. Justify selection of representative sizes and any normalization used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear relationship assumption for combined cycle efficiency with turbines <2,000 MMBtu/h
rubrics_metrics.description: “to estimate an achievable emissions rate for an efficient combined cycle EGU at 250 MMBtu/h the EPA assumed a linear relationship for combined cycle efficiency with turbine engines with base load ratings of less than 2,000 MMBtu/h.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating achievable emissions for smaller turbine sizes EPA used a linear interpolation/extrapolation of efficiency vs. base-load rating for engines under 2,000 MMBtu/h. Explicitly state and justify linearity assumptions when applying similar methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to determine facility emissions rate for a new small natural gas-fired base load EGU
rubrics_metrics.description: “As proposed, a new small natural gas-fired base load EGU would determine the facility emissions rate by taking the difference in the base load rating and 250 MMBtu/h, multiplying that number by 0.0743 lb CO2/(MW * MMBtu), and subtracting that number from 900 lb CO2/MWh-gross. The emissions rate for a natural gas-fired base load combustion turbine with a base load rating of 1,000 MMBtu/h is 900 lb CO2/MWh-gross minus 750 MMBtu/h (1,000 MMBtu/h-250 MMBtu/h) times 0.0743 lb CO2/(MW * MMBtu), which results in an emissions rate of 844 lb CO2/MWh-gross.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA prescribes a specific formula for facility emissions-rate calculation for this subcategory (base-load NG), including constants and example computation; use the same steps and constants to reproduce EPA's rate or explain deviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat-input-based emission-rate conversion between fuels
rubrics_metrics.description: “The heat input-based emission rates of natural gas and distillate oil are 117 and 163 lb CO2/MMBtu, respectively. The ratio of the heat input-based emission rates (1.39) is multiplied by the natural gas-fired standard of performance (770 lb CO2/MWh) to get the applicable emissions rate (1,070 lb CO2/MWh).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To convert an existing standard based on one fuel to an equivalent for another fuel, EPA multiplies by the ratio of fuel-specific heat-input CO2 intensities. Document the heat-input rates used and show the arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percent reduction from CCS accounts for increased auxiliary load (example: 89% vs 90%)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The 89 percent reduction from CCS accounts for the increased auxiliary load of a 90 percent post combustion amine-based capture system. Due to rounding, the proposed numeric standards of performance do not necessarily match the standards that would be determined by applying the percent reduction to the phase-1 standards.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stating percent reductions attributable to CCS, EPA adjusts capture percentages to reflect the capture technology’s parasitic load on the plant. Be aware of rounding differences between percent-based descriptions and numerically applied standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: CO2 transport and geologic sequestration reporting and monitoring requirements (mass-balance approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: “both subpart RR and subpart VV (CSA/ANSI ISO 27916:2019) require an assessment and monitoring of potential leakage pathways; quantification of inputs, losses, and storage through a mass balance approach; and documentation of steps and approaches used to establish these quantities. Primary differences relate to the terms in their respective mass balance equations, how each defines leakage, and when facilities may discontinue reporting.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For CO2 transport and storage, EPA expects (or references existing standards requiring) leakage-pathway assessment, mass-balance quantification of injections/losses/storage, and documentation of methods. Note that different regulatory frameworks (subpart RR vs CSA/ANSI ISO 27916/subpart VV) differ in mass-balance terms, leakage definitions, and criteria/timing for ending reporting; specify which framework is being used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of DOE/NETL, FEED studies, and expert interviews to validate cost estimates and technology readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: References to DOE/NETL cost models, FEED studies, Portfolio Insights: Carbon Capture in the Power Sector, NETL reports, and FEED/DOE analyses being used to compare and validate cost assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA relies on NETL and DOE FEED studies, DOE-funded FEED analyses, industry FEED results, and expert input to ground cost and technology-readiness estimates. When preparing cost or readiness assessments, reference equivalent up-to-date FEED/NETL/DOE analyses and explain adjustments for inflation, differing economic assumptions, and technical details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of operating profiles and future capacity factors when assessing compliance costs
rubrics_metrics.description: “The compliance costs assume the same capacity factors in the base and policy case, that is, without CCS and with CCS. If combined cycle turbine with CCS were to operate at higher capacity factors in the policy case, compliance costs would be reduced.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of compliance costs and cost-effectiveness should consider potential changes in operating profiles (e.g., higher capacity factors in policy scenarios, impacts of tax incentives) rather than assuming identical base- and policy-case capacity factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: HRSG configuration and exhaust-temperature considerations for efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the combustion turbine engine exhaust temperature is 500 °C or greater, a HRSG using 3 pressure steam without a reheat cycle could potentially provide an even greater increase in efficiency (relative to a HRSG using 2 pressure steam without a reheat cycle).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices (e.g., HRSG pressure levels and reheat) depend on turbine exhaust temperature; these choices affect achievable efficiency and should be considered when estimating achievable emissions and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition that CHP and useful thermal output can lower facility emissions rate
rubrics_metrics.description: “Combined cycle EGUs located in urban areas could be designed as CHP EGUs, which have potential environmental and economic benefits.... If the useful thermal output were accounted for, the emissions rate of the Holland Energy Park would be lower.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or benchmarking emissions rates, account for useful thermal outputs from CHP configurations where applicable, because including thermal credit lowers the effective electrical emissions rate.
